title: India Tells Starlink: Meet Security Rules, Build Local Base Stations First
excerpt: New Delhi says Elon Musk's satellite internet service has not yet agreed to compliance conditions every operator must meet, as Bharti's Sunil Mittal argues his OneWeb venture is ahead in the approval queue.
body:
• India says Starlink has not yet agreed to compliance conditions, including setting up local base stations, that satellite internet providers must meet before launching.
  • Three operators hold satcom licences — Starlink, Reliance Jio's satellite venture and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb — and each must individually clear security requirements, with the final call resting with the Ministry of Home Affairs.
  • Bharti Enterprises chair Sunil Bharti Mittal says OneWeb applied nearly five years ago and expects approval before Starlink.
  • For diaspora readers: satellite broadband is aimed at rural and remote India, where many NRI families' relatives still have no reliable high-speed connection.

Starlink has not yet received clearance to launch services in India because it has not agreed to comply with regulations requiring satellite internet providers to set up domestic infrastructure, a senior government official said on Wednesday. The message to Elon Musk was blunt: to do business in India, his company will have to abide by the law of the land, according to The Times of India.

Officials said the government has no objection to Starlink rolling out services once it addresses security concerns and agrees to establish local base stations before offering service. A base station acts as the local hub — the first hop connecting end-user devices to the wider network — and requiring it on Indian soil helps authorities secure compliance with Indian law.

A Public Spat Over Access

The compliance dispute has played out in public. Musk accused Indian telecom providers of preventing Starlink from entering the market, and the government denied his charge that Starlink was being discriminated against at the instance of a "local oligarch." Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has rejected the framing entirely, saying India does not allow monopolies in any sector and that security clearance is not the telecom ministry's call. As Scindia told reporters at the India Mobile Congress, according to Mint, the Ministry of Home Affairs must state that a company has shown compliance with the security requirements before operations can begin.

"I am significantly ahead in the queue from him. I applied five years back. I have my ground networks ready for three years."

— Sunil Bharti Mittal, Chairperson, Bharti Enterprises

Three Licensees, One Queue

Three entities are planning satellite communication services in India: Musk's Starlink, Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Jio satellite venture, and the Sunil Bharti Mittal-backed Eutelsat OneWeb. Scindia has stressed that all three hold licences and that each must individually fulfil security conditions and milestones; Amazon's Project Kuiper has also expressed interest and will have to follow the same process. Spectrum will be assigned administratively rather than auctioned, and the telecom regulator TRAI's recommended charge — 4% of adjusted gross revenue, proposed in May 2025 — is still awaiting a final decision the minister described as close.

Mittal, speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, argued that OneWeb deserves approval first: it applied nearly five years ago, its ground networks have been ready for three years, and its satellites have been positioned over India for five years. He said he would be "very happy" to receive approval at least a few days before Starlink.

Why It Matters Beyond the Boardroom

Satellite internet is not a prestige product in India; it is aimed squarely at terrain where fibre and mobile towers do not reach economically — Himalayan villages, island territories, remote districts in the Northeast and central India. For the diaspora, that coverage map overlaps heavily with the places many families come from. A working satcom market would mean video calls, telemedicine and digital banking reaching relatives in villages that broadband has so far skipped.

What Happens Next

Two gates remain. Each licensee must satisfy the home ministry on security compliance, and the government must finalise the revenue-based spectrum charge. Scindia has given no timeline for either. When both are cleared, the operators can start — in whatever order they qualify, not in the order they arrived in the headlines.
